title: Data
text: All files live in the data/ folder of this site and are loaded automatically into the browser’s Python and R. Download any of them with the links below to use locally. Genome build: GRCh38; annotation: GENCODE (as shipped in BIOL419 Lab 4, Spring 2026).

title: Data
text:
Where each file came from
COMT sequences and exons. Extracted from the chromosome 22 FASTA and GENCODE GTF used in BIOL419 Lab 4 (chr22.fa, chr22.gtf). The canonical transcript (Ensembl_canonical tag) was used; CDS segments were concatenated in genomic order (the gene is on the + strand) and the GTF stop_codon appended. Sanity checks performed: the translation starts with M, has exactly one stop at the end, and codon 158 is GTG (Val) at the position of rs4680 (chr22:19,963,748, GRCh38).
Reads. 5,000 records drawn at random (seed 405) from ENCFF729YAX_subset100k.fastq, a 100,000-read subset of ENCODE RNA-seq file ENCFF729YAX (HiSeq, 100-nt single-end) prepared for BIOL419 Lab 4. Immunoglobulin genes dominate the expression table, which points to a B-lymphocyte-derived sample.
chr22 genes. All gene records of the GENCODE chr22 GTF. length_bp is genomic span (end − start + 1), not transcript length.
chr22 expression. The sample_rsem.genes.results file produced in BIOL419 Lab 4 by STAR 2.7.10b → RSEM on the 100,000-read subset (see the handout in that lab). Columns kept: length (effective transcript length used by RSEM), expected_count, TPM. Because only chr22 was used as reference, TPM values are relative to chr22 only and are not comparable to whole-genome TPM.
chr22 mismatches. Derived from the STAR alignment (Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam) of the same 100,000 reads: for every aligned base with mapping quality ≥ 20 and base quality ≥ 20, the read base was compared with the reference; sites with depth ≥ 5 and ≥ 2 reads supporting the same alternative base are listed. gene_name is the protein-coding gene overlapping the site, if any. This is not a variant call set — it deliberately contains mis-mapping artefacts, reference differences and RNA editing sites, which is what Lab 1 Exercise 4c asks you to sort out.
airway. Himes BE et al. (2014) PLoS ONE 9:e99625, GEO GSE52778: four primary human airway smooth-muscle cell lines, each untreated and treated with 1 µM dexamethasone for 18 h. Counts are the gene-level table distributed with the Bioconductor airway package and used in the DESeq2 vignette; here filtered to genes with ≥ 10 reads in total. Sample IDs are SRA run accessions.

Exercise 2 · DNA as a string: COMT and rs4680 (20 min)
Run the setup cell for your language first (it defines read_fasta and reads the sequence into cds).


Python








R









2a · GC content
Fill in the blanks so the cell prints the GC content as a percentage.


Python













Hint





cds.count("C") counts C’s; len(cds) is the length.





g = cds.count("G")
c = cds.count("C")
gc = (g + c) / len(cds)
print(round(gc * 100, 1), "%")     # 61.8 %



R













Hint





%in% tests membership in a vector: c("G", "C").





bases <- strsplit(cds, "")[[1]]
gc <- mean(bases %in% c("G", "C"))
cat(round(gc * 100, 1), "%\n")     # 61.8 %




Both languages must print 61.8 %. The human genome averages about 41 % — COMT is a GC-rich gene on a GC-rich chromosome.



2b · Reverse complement
Write the reverse complement of cds and print its first 20 letters.


Python













Hint





reversed(cds) walks the string backwards.





complement = {"A": "T", "T": "A", "G": "C", "C": "G"}
rc = "".join(complement[b] for b in reversed(cds))
print(rc[:20])          # TCAGGGCCCTGCTTCGCTGC



R













Hint





complement[bases] looks up every base at once; rev() reverses a vector.





complement <- c(A = "T", T = "A", G = "C", C = "G")
rc <- paste(rev(complement[bases]), collapse = "")
cat(substr(rc, 1, 20), "\n")   # TCAGGGCCCTGCTTCGCTGC




The reverse complement must start with TCA — because the CDS ends with the stop codon TGA.



2c · Translate, then mutate codon 158
Run the setup cell (codon table + translate). Then complete the exercise: print codon 158 and its amino acid, change its first letter G→A (this is rs4680), and print the new amino acid.


Python



















Hint





Replace the first letter with "A". Amino acid 158 is index 157 in Python.





i = (158 - 1) * 3
codon = cds[i:i+3]
print("codon 158:", codon, "->", codon_table[codon])      # GTG -> V
mutant = cds[:i] + "A" + cds[i+1:]
print("mutant   :", mutant[i:i+3], "->", translate(mutant)[157])   # ATG -> M



R



















Hint





substr(x, i, i) <- "A" replaces one letter in place. Amino acid 158 is position 158 in R.





i <- (158 - 1) * 3 + 1
codon <- substr(cds, i, i + 2)
cat("codon 158:", codon, "->", codon_table[codon], "\n")    # GTG -> V
mutant <- cds
substr(mutant, i, i) <- "A"
cat("mutant   :", substr(mutant, i, i + 2), "->", substr(translate(mutant), 158, 158), "\n")  # ATG -> M




The protein must start with MPEAPPLLLA, be 271 aa long, and codon 158 must be GTG (V) → ATG (M). This is Val158Met, the COMT variant that lowers enzyme activity 3–4 fold.

How many amino acids now match the original before the sequence goes wrong, and where is the first stop codon? Explain in one sentence why a deletion is worse than a substitution.

5b · The 19,271-tests trap
Run a t-test on every gene. Count how many have p < 0.05. Then shuffle the sample labels and count again.


Python













Hint





0.05.

section: Exercise 1 · Is 16 of 20 evidence of imbalance? (10 min)
text:
Exercise 1 · Is 16 of 20 evidence of imbalance? (10 min)
A transcription factor’s ChIP-seq reads cover a heterozygous site: 16 reads from copy 1, 4 from copy 2. If the site is balanced, each read comes from copy 1 with probability 0.5. Test it, then compare three sites that all show 80 % copy 1 at different depths.


Python













Hint





The null hypothesis is a balanced site: 0.5.





for k, n in [(8, 10), (16, 20), (160, 200)]:
    r = stats.binomtest(k, n, 0.5)
    ci = r.proportion_ci()
    print(f"{k:>3} of {n:<3}  p = {r.pvalue:.2g}   95% CI {ci.low:.2f} - {ci.high:.2f}")
#   8 of 10   p = 0.11      95% CI 0.44 - 0.97
#  16 of 20   p = 0.012     95% CI 0.56 - 0.94
# 160 of 200  p = 3.4e-18   95% CI 0.74 - 0.85



R













Hint





The null hypothesis is a balanced site: p = 0.5.





for (x in list(c(8, 10), c(16, 20), c(160, 200))) {
  r <- binom.test(x[1], x[2], p = 0.5)
  cat(x[1], "of", x[2], " p =", signif(r$p.value, 2),
      "  95% CI", round(r$conf.int, 2), "\n")
}
# 8 of 10    p = 0.11     95% CI 0.44 0.97
# 16 of 20   p = 0.012    95% CI 0.56 0.94
# 160 of 200 p = 3.4e-18  95% CI 0.74 0.85




Same ratio, different evidence. Only 8 of 10 has an interval that still contains 0.5.

Q1. Why does 8 of 10 fail the test while 160 of 200, with the same 80 %, gives p = 3.4 × 10⁻¹⁸? Answer with the width of the 95 % interval.

Exercise 2 · One person, 100,000 tests (10 min)
A person has about 100,000 well-covered heterozygous sites. Suppose every one is balanced and each has 30 reads. How many still pass p < 0.05?
All sites have the same depth, so there are only 31 possible counts (0 to 30) and 31 possible p-values. We compute them once in a table and look each site up.


Python













Hint





0.05. Bonferroni divides 0.05 by the number of tests.





n, m = 30, 100_000
k = rng.binomial(n, 0.5, size=m)
pmf = stats.binom.pmf(np.arange(n + 1), n, 0.5)
p_table = np.array([two_sided(x, n, pmf) for x in range(n + 1)])
p = p_table[k]
print("p < 0.05:        ", (p < 0.05).sum())          # about 4,300-4,400
print("Bonferroni line: ", 0.05 / m, "->", (p < 0.05 / m).sum(), "sites")   # 0



R













Hint





0.05. Note p_table[k + 1]: R vectors start at position 1.





n <- 30; m <- 100000
k <- rbinom(m, n, 0.5)
pmf <- dbinom(0:n, n, 0.5)
p_table <- sapply(0:n, function(x) two_sided(x, n, pmf))
p <- p_table[k + 1]
cat("p < 0.05:        ", sum(p < 0.05), "\n")             # about 4,300-4,400
cat("Bonferroni line: ", 0.05 / m, "->", sum(p < 0.05 / m), "sites\n")   # 0




About 4,300–4,400 balanced sites pass p < 0.05, all false. None passes the Bonferroni line of 5 × 10⁻⁷. (The exact count changes from run to run, and Python and R draw different random numbers.)

Q2. Why is the count a little below 5 % of 100,000? (Look at p_table: can a count of 30 reads give a p-value of exactly 0.05?)

title: Lab 2 · Statistics in personal and population genomics
section: Exercise 3 · A balanced site that looks imbalanced (25 min)
text:
Exercise 3 · A balanced site that looks imbalanced (25 min)
The story, one site at a time:

The truth. The factor binds both copies equally: 50 / 50.
A technical factor tips the balance. During library preparation, PCR happens to copy fragments from copy 1 more often. The 20 reads now come from a pool that is 75 % copy 1.
The data. We see 16 reads from copy 1 and 4 from copy 2.
The binomial test (Exercise 1) says p = 0.012: “significant”. The conclusion is wrong: the imbalance came from the experiment, not the biology.


3a · How ordinary is 16 of 20 from a 75 % pool?


Python








R








Under the pool the experiment actually made, 16 or more happens 41 % of the time. The binomial test is fooled because it assumes p is exactly 0.5 in every experiment.


3b · Add a layer: let p stray, by an amount we do not know
We keep the coin flips, but we stop fixing p. Each experiment draws its own p from a Beta(α, β) distribution, and then the reads are drawn as before. This two-layer model is the beta-binomial.



The binomial (top) and the beta-binomial (second row) differ only in the first box. Bottom left: three beliefs about how far p may stray. Bottom right: the read counts each belief expects at a balanced site.


What α and β mean. Think of them as imaginary reads we hold in mind before seeing any data: α from copy 1 and β from copy 2.

Their ratio sets the centre. The average p is α / (α + β). Setting α = β keeps the centre at 0.5: the biology is balanced.
Their sum sets how sure we are. A large α + β gives a narrow Beta, so p stays near 0.5. A small sum gives a wide Beta, so p can stray far.




Choice
What it says
Typical spread of p (SD)




p exactly 0.5 (binomial)
no technical noise
0


Beta(50, 50)
very little noise
0.05


Beta(9.5, 9.5)
some technical noise
0.11


Beta(1, 1)
no idea: any p equally likely
0.29



Draw the Beta curves yourself. Change α and β, then run again.


Python













Hint





The flat Beta is 1.





x = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 2.8))
for a in [50, 9.5, 1]:
    ax.plot(x, stats.beta.pdf(x, a, a), label=f"Beta({a}, {a})")
ax.set_xlabel("p, this experiment's fraction from copy 1"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for a in [50, 9.5, 1]:
    print(f"Beta({a}, {a}): SD of p = {stats.beta.std(a, a):.3f}")   # 0.050, 0.112, 0.289



R













Hint





The flat Beta is dbeta(x, 1, 1).





x <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 400)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(x, dbeta(x, 50, 50), type = "l", ylim = c(0, 8),
     xlab = "p, this experiment's fraction from copy 1", ylab = "density")
lines(x, dbeta(x, 9.5, 9.5), col = "blue")
lines(x, dbeta(x, 1, 1), col = "orange")
sd_beta <- function(a) sqrt(a * a / ((2 * a)^2 * (2 * a + 1)))
cat("SD of p:", round(sapply(c(50, 9.5, 1), sd_beta), 3), "\n")   # 0.050 0.112 0.289





3c · Test 16 of 20 again, now allowing p to stray
Use the beta-binomial distribution of counts in place of the binomial, and compute the same two-sided p-value.


Python













Hint





α = β, so the fourth argument is a again.





n, k = 20, 16
counts = np.arange(n + 1)
print("binomial        p =", round(two_sided(k, n, stats.binom.pmf(counts, n, 0.5)), 3))
for a in [50, 9.5, 1]:
    pmf = stats.betabinom.pmf(counts, n, a, a)
    print(f"Beta({a}, {a})".ljust(15), "p =", round(two_sided(k, n, pmf), 3))
# binomial 0.012 · Beta(50, 50) 0.021 · Beta(9.5, 9.5) 0.076 · Beta(1, 1) 0.476



R













Hint





α = β, so the last argument is a again.





n <- 20; k <- 16
cat("binomial        p =", round(two_sided(k, n, dbinom(0:n, n, 0.5)), 3), "\n")
for (a in c(50, 9.5, 1)) {
  pmf <- dbetabinom(0:n, n, a, a)
  cat("Beta(", a, ",", a, ")  p =", round(two_sided(k, n, pmf), 3), "\n")
}
# binomial 0.012 · Beta(50, 50) 0.021 · Beta(9.5, 9.5) 0.076 · Beta(1, 1) 0.476




With some technical noise allowed for (Beta(9.5, 9.5)), 16 of 20 is not significant (p = 0.076). Allow too much (Beta(1, 1)) and nothing can ever be called (p = 0.48).



3d · From one site to many
Every heterozygous site in a dataset goes through the same library preparation, so each one gets its own random push. Simulate 10,000 balanced sites this way: draw each site’s p from Beta(9.5, 9.5), then draw 20 reads. Test every site with both models.


Python













Hint





Each site uses its own p: p_site.





n, m, a = 20, 10_000, 9.5
p_site = rng.beta(a, a, size=m)
k = rng.binomial(n, p_site)
counts = np.arange(n + 1)
p_binom = np.array([two_sided(x, n, stats.binom.pmf(counts, n, 0.5)) for x in counts])[k]
p_bb    = np.array([two_sided(x, n, stats.betabinom.pmf(counts, n, a, a)) for x in counts])[k]
print("balanced sites called significant (p < 0.05)")
print("  binomial:     ", round((p_binom < 0.05).mean() * 100, 1), "%")   # about 15 %
print("  beta-binomial:", round((p_bb < 0.05).mean() * 100, 1), "%")      # about 3 %



R













Hint





Each site uses its own p: p_site.





n <- 20; m <- 10000; a <- 9.5
p_site <- rbeta(m, a, a)
k <- rbinom(m, n, p_site)
tab_binom <- sapply(0:n, function(x) two_sided(x, n, dbinom(0:n, n, 0.5)))
tab_bb    <- sapply(0:n, function(x) two_sided(x, n, dbetabinom(0:n, n, a, a)))
cat("balanced sites called significant (p < 0.05)\n")
cat("  binomial:     ", round(mean(tab_binom[k + 1] < 0.05) * 100, 1), "%\n")   # about 15 %
cat("  beta-binomial:", round(mean(tab_bb[k + 1] < 0.05) * 100, 1), "%\n")      # about 3 %




All 10,000 sites are balanced. The binomial calls about 15 % of them significant; the beta-binomial about 3 %, below the 5 % a correct test promises.

Q3. In 3c you had to choose α and β. In real data we cannot repeat one site’s experiment many times, so one site gives a single count. Explain in two sentences why α and β are estimated from all heterozygous sites of a dataset together, and why that works (think of 3d).

title: Lab 2 · Statistics in personal and population genomics
text:
Exercise 4 · Hardy–Weinberg at rs2814778 (15 min)
rs2814778 (ACKR1, the Duffy blood group) has alleles T (frequency p) and C (frequency q = 1 − p). These are the real genotype counts in the 2,504 people of 1000 Genomes, by continental group. Lecture 13 showed that the whole cohort fails Hardy–Weinberg badly. Test each group on its own.


Python













Hint





Heterozygotes are expected at frequency 2 * p * q.





pops = pd.read_csv("data/lab2/rs2814778_by_population.tsv", sep="\t")

def hwe(TT, CT, CC):
    n = TT + CT + CC
    p = (2 * TT + CT) / (2 * n)
    q = 1 - p
    expected = n * np.array([p**2, 2 * p * q, q**2])
    observed = np.array([TT, CT, CC])
    keep = expected > 0
    chi2 = (((observed - expected) ** 2 / np.where(keep, expected, 1))[keep]).sum()
    return round(p, 3), np.round(expected, 1), round(chi2, 1), stats.chi2.sf(chi2, df=1)

print("ALL", hwe(*pops[["TT", "CT", "CC"]].sum()))
for _, r in pops.iterrows():
    print(r["population"], hwe(r["TT"], r["CT"], r["CC"]))
# ALL chi2 2073.9 · AFR 12.1 (p = 5e-4) · AMR 8.5 · EAS 0 · EUR 0.0 · SAS 0



R













Hint





Heterozygotes are expected at frequency 2 * p * q.





pops <- read.delim("data/lab2/rs2814778_by_population.tsv")

hwe <- function(TT, CT, CC) {
  n <- TT + CT + CC
  p <- (2 * TT + CT) / (2 * n)
  q <- 1 - p
  expected <- n * c(p^2, 2 * p * q, q^2)
  observed <- c(TT, CT, CC)
  keep <- expected > 0
  chi2 <- sum(((observed - expected)^2 / expected)[keep])
  c(p = round(p, 3), round(expected, 1), chi2 = round(chi2, 1),
    pvalue = signif(pchisq(chi2, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE), 2))
}

hwe(sum(pops$TT), sum(pops$CT), sum(pops$CC))
by_group <- t(sapply(1:nrow(pops), function(i) hwe(pops$TT[i], pops$CT[i], pops$CC[i])))
rownames(by_group) <- pops$population
by_group
# rows: AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR, SAS · chi2 12.1, 8.5, 0, 0.0, 0




Pooled: χ² = 2,074. Within groups the failure shrinks to χ² = 12.1 (AFR) and 8.5 (AMR); EUR fits (χ² ≈ 0). In EAS and SAS everyone is TT, so there is nothing to test.

Q4. Splitting by group removed almost all of the failure. Why do AFR and AMR still fail a little? (Hint: each of these continental groups combines several populations, some of them of recently mixed ancestry, such as African Americans in the southwest US (ASW) and Puerto Ricans (PUR).)

title: Lab 2 · Statistics in personal and population genomics
section: Exercise 5 · A GWAS of one region (15 min)
text:
Exercise 5 · A GWAS of one region (15 min)
gwas_region.tsv has 2,000 people, 15 SNPs spread over 190 kb, and a trait. Run the GWAS regression at every SNP: trait = a + β × genotype. Compute z = β / SE, the p-value, and draw the region with the genome-wide line at 5 × 10⁻⁸.


Python













Hint





z is the slope divided by its standard error: fit.stderr.





gw   = pd.read_csv("data/lab2/gwas_region.tsv", sep="\t")
snps = pd.read_csv("data/lab2/gwas_snps.tsv", sep="\t")
rows = []
for s in snps["snp"]:
    fit = stats.linregress(gw[s], gw["trait"])
    z = fit.slope / fit.stderr
    rows.append([s, round(fit.slope, 3), round(fit.stderr, 4), round(z, 2), fit.pvalue])
res = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["snp", "beta", "se", "z", "p"])
res["position"] = snps["position"]
print(res.to_string(index=False))
# lead: snp8, beta 0.261, SE 0.0338, z 7.72, p 1.8e-14
# snp6, snp7, snp9, snp10 also pass 5e-8; snp12 and snp14 have p = 0.04

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 2.8))
ax.scatter(res["position"] / 1e6, -np.log10(res["p"]))
ax.axhline(-np.log10(5e-8), color="red", ls="--")
ax.set_xlabel("position (Mb)"); ax.set_ylabel("-log10 p")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



R













Hint





z is the slope divided by its standard error: co[["Std. Error"]].





gw   <- read.delim("data/lab2/gwas_region.tsv")
snps <- read.delim("data/lab2/gwas_snps.tsv")
res <- t(sapply(snps$snp, function(s) {
  co <- summary(lm(gw$trait ~ gw[[s]]))$coefficients[2, ]
  c(beta = co[["Estimate"]], se = co[["Std. Error"]],
    z = co[["Estimate"]] / co[["Std. Error"]], p = co[["Pr(>|t|)"]])
}))
res <- data.frame(res, position = snps$position)
print(cbind(signif(res[, 1:4], 3), position = res$position))
# lead: snp8, beta 0.261, SE 0.0338, z 7.72, p 1.8e-14

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(res$position / 1e6, -log10(res$p), pch = 19,
     xlab = "position (Mb)", ylab = "-log10 p")
abline(h = -log10(5e-8), col = "red", lty = 2)



Now measure linkage: r² between the lead SNP and every other SNP is the squared correlation of their genotype columns.


Python








R









Five neighbouring SNPs (snp6–snp10) pass 5 × 10⁻⁸; their r² with snp8 is 0.57–0.93. In this simulation only snp8 affects the trait. Two SNPs in another block have p ≈ 0.04: below 0.05, far above the genome-wide line.

Q5. (a) From the results alone, could you tell which of snp6–snp10 is the causal one? Why or why not? (b) Why is p = 0.04 at snp12 not a finding in a GWAS?

title: Lab 2 · Statistics in personal and population genomics
section: Exercise 6 · Group differences create a false hit (10 min)
text:
Exercise 6 · Group differences create a false hit (10 min)
stratification.tsv: 1,000 people from two groups. The allele frequency is about 0.2 in group 1 and 0.7 in group 2, and the trait is higher in group 2 for a non-genetic reason. The SNP has no effect on the trait. Run the GWAS regression without, then with, the group in the model.


Python













Hint





Add the group indicator in_group2 as a second column.





st = pd.read_csv("data/lab2/stratification.tsv", sep="\t")
print(st.groupby("group").agg(freq=("genotype", lambda g: g.mean() / 2),
                              mean_trait=("trait", "mean")))

def ols(columns, y):
    """least squares; returns beta, SE and p for every column after the intercept"""
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y))] + columns)
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    resid = y - X @ beta
    df = len(y) - X.shape[1]
    se = np.sqrt(np.diag(resid @ resid / df * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)))
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(beta / se), df)
    return np.round(beta[1:], 3), np.round(se[1:], 4), p[1:]

g = st["genotype"].to_numpy(float)
y = st["trait"].to_numpy()
in_group2 = (st["group"] == 2).to_numpy(float)
print("trait ~ genotype:         ", ols([g], y))
print("trait ~ genotype + group: ", ols([g, in_group2], y))
# genotype only: beta 0.373, p 3e-18
# with group:    beta 0.061, p 0.25   (group effect 0.768)



R













Hint





factor(group) tells R the group is a category, not a number.





st <- read.delim("data/lab2/stratification.tsv")
print(aggregate(cbind(freq = genotype / 2, trait) ~ group, data = st, FUN = mean))
m1 <- lm(trait ~ genotype, data = st)
m2 <- lm(trait ~ genotype + factor(group), data = st)
summary(m1)$coefficients["genotype", ]   # beta 0.373, p 3e-18
summary(m2)$coefficients["genotype", ]   # beta 0.061, p 0.25




Without the group: β = 0.373, p = 3 × 10⁻¹⁸, a “genome-wide hit” for a SNP that does nothing. With the group in the model: β = 0.061, p = 0.25.

Q6. Explain in your own words why the SNP looked associated with the trait. In a real GWAS, people do not come labelled with a group: what do studies put in the model instead? (Lecture 13.)
Q7. Exercise 3 and Exercise 6 have the same shape: a hidden factor makes an ordinary test too confident, and the fix adds that factor to the model. Name the hidden factor and the fix in each.

title: Lecture 10 · Programming for Biologists: Python and R
text:
Part 1 · Why two languages?
Python (Guido van Rossum, 1991) was designed as a general-purpose language that reads like pseudocode. When DNA sequencing started producing text at scale (2005–2010), Python’s string handling and its “glue” nature made it the language of pipelines: reads, files, tools, web services.
R (Ross Ihaka & Robert Gentleman, University of Auckland, 1993) is the open-source descendant of S (John Chambers, Bell Labs, 1976), a language built for statistics. In 2001 Bioconductor was founded on R, and since then most statistical methods for genomics (limma, edgeR, DESeq2) have been published as R packages first.









Python
R




Born
1991, general purpose
1993, statistics (from S, 1976)


Natural unit
string, list, dict
vector, data frame


Genomics home
Biopython, pysam, scanpy, PyTorch
Bioconductor: DESeq2, edgeR, Seurat


Plots
matplotlib (a library)
plot() is built into the language


Where you meet it
pipelines, machine learning, web
statistics, figures for the paper



Neither is “the real one”. A typical genomics project runs a Python (or shell) pipeline to produce a table of counts, then an R notebook to test hypotheses and draw the figures.

title: Lecture 10 · Programming for Biologists: Python and R
text:
Part 2 · Same idea, two syntaxes
The first thing to learn is that the differences are mostly surface. Here is the same tiny program.


Python








R









The four differences that actually matter

Indexing starts at 0 in Python and at 1 in R. dna[0] in Python is the first letter; substr(dna, 1, 1) in R is the first letter. Half of all coordinate bugs in genomics come from this. (BED files are 0-based; GTF/VCF files are 1-based.)
Python works on one string; R works on vectors. In R, almost everything is a vector, so mean(bases %in% c("G","C")) computes GC content without a loop. Python needs a loop or str.count.
Assignment: = in Python, <- in R (R also accepts =).
Blocks: Python uses indentation; R uses { }.


In the cells above, change the sequence to "ATGAAATTT" and predict the GC content before you run.

title: Lecture 10 · Programming for Biologists: Python and R
text:
Part 3 · Biology as strings
The coding sequence of COMT (catechol-O-methyltransferase, chromosome 22) is 816 letters. We will read it from a FASTA file, then do what every sequence tool does: count, reverse-complement, translate.


Python








R









Reverse complement
DNA is double-stranded; a read may come from either strand. The reverse complement is reverse the string, then complement each letter.


Python








R










The genetic code is a dictionary
64 codons → 21 outcomes (20 amino acids + stop). In Python this is a dict; in R it is a named vector. The string below lists the amino acids in the standard TCAG order.


Python








R










One letter, one amino acid: rs4680 (Val158Met)
The most studied variant in COMT is rs4680: a G→A change in codon 158 that turns valine (GTG) into methionine (ATG) and reduces enzyme activity 3–4 fold. The reference genome carries the G. Watch the off-by-one:


Python








R









Python cds[471:474] and R substr(cds, 472, 474) are the same three letters. If you copy a 1-based coordinate from a VCF or GTF file into Python without subtracting 1, you translate the wrong codon and never notice.

text:
Part 7 · Working like a scientist

Ecosystems. Python packages come from PyPI (pip install) or conda; R packages from CRAN (install.packages) and Bioconductor (BiocManager::install("DESeq2")). A tool published in a paper is usually on one of these.
Notebooks are lab notebooks. Jupyter (.ipynb) and Quarto/R Markdown (.qmd, .Rmd) keep code, output and your comments together. This website is a Quarto document.
Reproducibility. Record versions (pip freeze, sessionInfo()), set random seeds, never edit raw data by hand, keep the script that made every figure.
ChatGPT writes code; you verify it. Use TRACE prompting, then run the code on a case you already know the answer to — COMT codon 158 must be GTG; the protein must start with M — before you trust it on new data.


The five bugs that bit real papers

0-based vs 1-based coordinates (BED vs GTF/VCF).
Strand: a k-mer from the minus strand never matches unless you reverse-complement.
Reference build: GRCh37 positions pasted into a GRCh38 file (rs4680 is chr22:19,963,748 in GRCh38 but 19,951,271 in GRCh37).
Excel turns gene names into dates: SEPT7 → “7-Sep”, MARCH1 → “1-Mar”. About one fifth of published supplementary gene lists contain this error (Ziemann et al. 2016), which is why HGNC renamed these genes in 2020 (SEPTIN7, MARCHF1).
Silent type coercion: a column read as text because one row says “NA”; a p-value column sorted as strings (“1e-10” after “0.5”).

0 · The coin, the p-value, and the burden of many tests
Before any genomics: three ideas, each with an experiment you can run here.

A coin flipped 10 times


Python








R








Nothing about the coin changes between experiments; the spread is what randomness looks like. A read covering a heterozygous site is the same coin: each read comes from one of the two chromosomes.


Is this coin fair? — the p-value
I flip a coin 10 times and get 9 heads. Null hypothesis: the coin is fair. p-value: how often a fair coin gives a result at least this extreme (9 or 10 heads, or by symmetry 0 or 1).


Python








R








p ≈ 0.02: chance alone does this about twice in a hundred. It is a statement about the data given the null, not the probability that the coin is fair.


Twenty candy colours, 19,271 genes — the burden
Test 20 candy colours for a link to acne when none exists: each test has a 1-in-20 chance of a false alarm, so the chance that at least one colour “wins” is 1 − 0.95²⁰ = 64 %. Now do it for every gene:


Python








R








Under the null, p-values are spread evenly: about 5 % fall below 0.05 — 800–960 false “discoveries” with nothing going on. Two ways to pay:

Bonferroni — control the chance of any false alarm: threshold 0.05 / 19,271 ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻⁶. Right for 20 candy colours; throws away almost everything in a genome.
False discovery rate (Benjamini–Hochberg, 1995) — control the fraction of false alarms in your list. Sort the p-values; the k-th smallest is kept if p₍ₖ₎ ≤ q·k/n. “Of the genes I call, about 5 % are expected to be false” — a promise about the list, not about one gene. p.adjust(p, "BH") returns the smallest FDR at which each gene would be kept (DESeq2’s padj).

text:
1 · Sequencing is sampling
A sequencer does not measure a gene’s expression; it draws reads at random from a pool of molecules. Every number in genomics is therefore a count from a random sample, and every claim needs a probability model.
Three distributions cover most of genomics:








Question
Model
Where




Of n reads at a site, how many carry allele A?
Binomial(n, θ)
genotyping, allele-specific expression, RNA editing


How many reads land in a window / on a gene?

coverage (Lander–Waterman), ChIP-seq peaks (MACS)


Same, but across biological replicates?
Negative binomial(μ, α)
RNA-seq differential expression (DESeq2, edgeR)




Binomial: is this mismatch a heterozygous SNP?
In Lab 1 you found a site with 54 alt reads out of 138. If the sample were heterozygous (θ = 0.5), how surprising is 54/138?


Python








R










Poisson: why 25 reads in one window is a peak
If reads fell uniformly, a 500-bp window that receives λ = 5 reads on average would receive 25 reads with probability:


Python








R








This is the core of a peak caller: MACS computes a local λ from the control (input or mock) and asks the Poisson question at every window. The whole difficulty is choosing the right λ — that is Section 6.


Negative binomial: replicates are noisier than Poisson
For a Poisson variable, variance = mean. Look at the four control samples of the airway experiment.


Python








R








95 % of genes have variance above the Poisson line. The extra variance is biological (four different people). The negative binomial adds one parameter, the dispersion α: variance = μ + α μ². DESeq2’s job is to estimate α for every gene from only a handful of replicates.

section: 2 · Estimation: likelihood and the EM idea
text:
2 · Estimation: likelihood and the EM idea
Maximum likelihood. Given data, choose the parameter that makes the data most probable. For a binomial with 54 of 138, the MLE is θ̂ = 54/138 = 0.39 — the obvious answer, now justified.
Bayes. Multiply the likelihood by a prior and normalize: with a flat prior, θ | data ~ Beta(54 + 1, 84 + 1). Now we can ask P(θ > 0.5), which a p-value cannot answer. Section 6 uses exactly this.
EM. When some data are hidden (which transcript did a shared read come from?), alternate: E-step — assign hidden labels in expectation using the current parameters; M-step — re-estimate parameters from the assigned data. Repeat until nothing changes.

EM in ten lines (the RSEM idea)
Two transcripts, A and B. 6 reads map only to A, 2 only to B, 4 map to both. What are the abundances?


Python








R








Naive “split 50/50” gives A = 8/12 = 0.667. EM converges to 0.75 / 0.25: because A is more abundant, the shared reads more likely came from A, which makes A more abundant still — until the answer is self-consistent. This is what RSEM does across all isoforms of all genes with all multi-mapping reads; its expected_count column is the E-step’s final assignment (which is why chr22_expression.tsv has counts like 317.84).

4 · Testing: from one t-test to DESeq2
What a t-test assumes that counts violate: normal errors with equal variance, independence between the 8 samples (but samples come in 4 donor pairs), and one test at a time.
What DESeq2 does (Love, Huber & Anders, Genome Biology 2014):

Model each gene’s count as NB(μ, α) with log μ = log(size factor) + β·design. The design ~ cell + dex handles the pairing.
Estimate each gene’s dispersion α, then shrink it toward the trend of α vs mean across all genes — borrowing strength, because 4 vs 4 is not enough to estimate a variance well.
Fit the GLM; test β_dex = 0 with a Wald test (or a likelihood-ratio test).
Adjust p-values with Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR).
Optionally shrink log2 fold changes (lfcShrink) so that low-count genes do not top the list.


Multiple testing: BH by hand


Python








R








The t-test keeps ~40 genes after correction. DESeq2 on the same data (with ~ cell + dex) reports several thousand at FDR 0.1 — not because it is lenient, but because the NB model with shrunken dispersion and the paired design have far more power. That gap is the whole reason to learn the model.






DESeq2 itself does not run in the browser (it is a Bioconductor package). On your laptop: BiocManager::install("DESeq2"), then dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cts, meta, ~ cell + dex); dds <- DESeq(dds); res <- results(dds). The Setup page has the full script.

title: Lecture 11 · Probability and Statistics for Genomic Data
text:
5 · ChIP-seq: designing the null
A ChIP-seq signal = specific binding (antibody × target TF) + non-specific binding (antibody × other proteins, open chromatin) + sonication bias (open chromatin shears more easily). A peak caller compares IP to a control and asks the Poisson question. Which control?

DNA input (sonicated chromatin, no antibody): corrects sonication bias only. Lots of DNA → deep, low-noise library.
Mock IP (IgG or no-target antibody, full IP protocol): corrects sonication bias and non-specific binding. Very little DNA → shallow, noisy library.


What “To mock or not” found (Xu et al., NAR 2021)
Using modERN datasets with matched IP, input and mock IP — 113 human (6 cell lines), 317 worm and 182 fly experiments:

Mock IP removes far more spurious sites than input: about 10 % of input-called peaks in human cell lines, but ~60 % in worm and ~88 % in fly (whole animals, many cell types).
Peaks that survive mock IP are more often real: motif enrichment rises 18–37 % in the top peaks.
But mock IP libraries are shallow and noisy, so used alone they lose sensitivity.
Recommendation: use both. Call peaks against input (sensitivity), then score each peak by how much stronger IP is than mock — a Bayesian posterior that uses all four libraries.



The posterior probability, in code
For a region with n_i reads in IP and n_d in input, θ₁ = IP fraction ~ Beta(n_i + 1, n_d + 1). For the mock experiment (n_m in mock IP, n_d’ in its input), θ₂ ~ Beta(n_m + 1, n_d’ + 1). A genuine peak needs θ₁ > 0.5 (enriched over input) and θ₁ > θ₂ (more enriched than mock). The paper computes P(θ₁ > 0.5 & θ₁ > θ₂) by integration; here we do it by simulation.


Python








R








Same IP enrichment (40 vs 10) in both cases. When the mock IP is also enriched (30 vs 10), the posterior drops to ~0.7 — a “hyper-ChIPable” region where any antibody pulls down DNA. When the mock is flat (5 vs 10), the posterior is ~1: a real peak.
